newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Brazil's Garantia bank raises eyebrows.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Brazil's Garantia bank raises eyebrows.

text.p: Its aggressive business tactics may raise eyebrows throughout world markets, but when it comes to making money in Latin America, few do it better than Brazil's Banco de Investimentos Garantia.
Whether trading bonds, speculating on dollar futures or simply brewing beer, Garantia's team of investment bankers does so with an agility recognised by rivals at home and abroad.
"We're very impressed with their ability in the marketplace. They are very capable and worthy of respect," said Gordon Tanner, a vice president at Salomon Brothers in New York.
PIONEER OF INVESTMENT BANKING IN BRAZIL

Garantia, one of Latin America's fastest-growing financial institutions, was founded in 1971 as a brokerage house in Rio de Janeiro and became an investment bank in 1976. It helped pioneer the business in Brazil, whose large economy and sophisticated markets have made it Latin America's only country to develop a strong investment banking sector.

Jorge Lemann, a five-time Brazilian tennis champion who once played at Wimbledon, is the only original partner still with Garantia. Lemann has pulled away from the bank's day-to-day activities, which are under the direction of chief executive officer Claudio Haddad.

In 1990, Garantia moved its headquarters to Brazil's sprawling industrial and financial capital of Sao Paulo, where it has developed a reputation for being a fiercely competitive player in Brazilian financial markets.
"You don't want to bet against them unless you're 100 percent sure," said a trader at a large Brazilian retail bank.

Garantia's net profits have soared in the past few years, growing an impressive 44 percent in 1995 to $105 million. Earnings are expected to rise to $120 million this year on working capital of about $500 million. The bank, with 320 people on its payroll, has total assets of $4.5 billion.
REASONS FOR SUCCESS DEBATED

Some analysts say Garantia's enormous success would not have been possible without Brazil's return to world capital markets and economic stability. They note that competitors like Rio de Janeiro's Banco Pactual, Banco Icatu and Banco Bozano Simonsen have emerged to give Garanatia a run for its money.
Garantia's detractors, many of them competitors who routinely lose out to the bank on the trading floor, also complain that its tactics at times move beyond fair play.

A recent spat with the Argentine government highlighted charges, always denied by Garantia, that its traders often pepper the market with rumours in an attempt to strengthen the bank's investment positions.

In late July Roque Fernandez, the newly appointed Argentine Economy Minister, was forced to deny market talk that Buenos Aires planned to abandon its internationally respected exchange system of peso-dollar parity.
Fernandez denounced the rumour as an "unethical" attempt by market players to move prices and pledged to punish the "international bank that started the talk."
Although Fernandez never named the guilty party, Garantia was vilified the next day by the Argentine press, which reported that the rumour had been traced back to the bank.
"It's absolutely ridiculous to think we started the rumour," Haddad told Reuters, adding that Garantia's research team took the opposite position.
Haddad said the Argentine authorities had never contacted Garantia about the incident. "But as a matter of courtesy, and to set the record straight, we sent them our research report."
RESEARCH RAISES EYEBROWS

Shortly after the Argentine incident, Garantia downgraded Brazil's benchmark stock Telebras to a hold from a buy, when virtually all other brokerages were bullish about the state telephone company's earnings prospects.
Many players read it as a deliberate attempt by Garantia to bend its research division to the whims of the trading floor.
"Our analyst discovered something nobody else had paid attention to," Haddad said. "We discovered a relevant fact and pointed it out to the market."

Haddad said the analyst determined that Telebras faced a potential liability from the privatisation of a cellular service under proposed legislation. The issue is still pending. Other investment banks, however, said the point made was not well-founded and maintained their ratings on Telebras.

The bank admits it is highly competitive when it comes to securing underwriting deals or trading in large volumes to support its market position. "We are no more aggressive than any U.S. investment bank. The problem is that we are perhaps more aggressive than the average Brazilian institution," Haddad said.
He added that Garantia traders have been fined for foul play only once by Brazil's securities and exchange commission.
SUCCESS BEYOND STOCKS AND BONDS
Outside Brazil, Garantia has made a name for itself in Brazilian sovereign debt, having traded some $50 billion of the nation's Brady bonds so far this year.

In 1992, Garantia became the first Brazilian investment bank to open offices in New York, where it competes head-on with J.P. Morgan, ING Bank, Salomon Brothers and other top players in emerging market debt.
At home, Garantia focuses on corporate finance and is a leader in mergers, acquisitions and underwriting securities.
But the Garantia team boasts considerable acumen in non-financial activities as well.

Senior partners control Brazil's giant beverage company Brahma, which under their guidance has grown into the world's fifth largest brewery. Garantia partners also control Lojas Americanas, the country's largest non-food retailer, which has teamed up with Wal-Mart to open megastores in suburban Brazil.
OPERATING STYLE PAYS LITTLE HEED TO TRADITION
No one stands out as the single driving force behind Garantia, which prides itself on a meritocratic structure that rewards teamwork and pays little heed to tradition.

With no formal dress code, traders frequently show up to work in bluejeans and polo shirts. The bank provides no separate offices for senior partners, who work alongside junior staff in one large trading room.

Client visits are held in spartan meeting rooms, devoid of artwork, expensive furniture and other frills traditionally found in bank offices. Garantia business cards carry no titles below the names of bank employees, including its senior partners. Even Haddad avoids using his CEO title.
"We all like to think of ourselves as associates," he said.
Despite Garantia's informal culture, the work environment is rigorous. With nearly half of all new hires leaving in the first 18 months, it is imperative new recruits learn the ropes fast.
"We are always hiring new people," said Hadded. "It is a demanding job."
